decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: Near light rail power lines, what should children not fly?
cards.back: Children should not fly kites or model airplanes near the overhead power lines used by light rail.

cards.front: Is skateboarding, rollerblading or bike riding allowed on light rail tracks or platforms?
cards.back: Skateboarding, rollerblading and bike riding on light rail tracks or station platforms is unsafe and not permitted.

cards.front: Which traffic laws do bicyclists follow, and when do they get the right-of-way?
cards.back: Bicyclists must follow the same traffic laws as drivers, and they get the right-of-way in the same situations that drivers do.

cards.front: Why must drivers use extra caution around bicyclists?
cards.back: Bicyclists are often hard to see, so drivers must watch for them along the road and use extra caution.

cards.front: When passing a bicyclist going your direction, how much space must you leave?
cards.back: When passing a bicyclist who is going the same direction, a driver must leave a safe distance of at least three feet.

cards.front: Why is honking at a bicyclist while you pass unsafe?
cards.back: Honking at a bicyclist while you pass is unsafe because the sound may startle the rider and cause a crash.

cards.front: What courtesy should you give bicyclists with your headlights at night?
cards.back: At night, dim your headlights as a courtesy to bicyclists.

cards.front: For what reasons may a bicyclist legally move left?
cards.back: Be ready for a bicyclist to swerve, because a rider may legally move left to turn left, avoid a hazard, pass a pedestrian or vehicle, or when the lane is too narrow to share safely.

cards.front: Bicyclists ride near the right, but when may they legally move left?
cards.back: Bicyclists normally ride with traffic near the right side, yet they may legally move left to turn left, avoid a hazard, pass, or when the lane is too narrow to share.

decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: In which direction must bicyclists ride?
cards.back: Bicyclists must ride in the same direction as traffic.

cards.front: How many people may a bicycle carry?
cards.back: A bicycle may not carry more people than it was designed to carry.

cards.front: How many bicyclists may ride side by side?
cards.back: Bicyclists may not ride more than two abreast.

cards.front: Where on the road should bicyclists ride?
cards.back: Bicyclists should ride as close to the right side of the road as is practicable.

cards.front: How should bicyclists signal?
cards.back: Bicyclists should use proper hand signals.

cards.front: Is riding a bicycle under the influence of drugs or alcohol legal?
cards.back: Riding a bicycle under the influence of drugs or alcohol is illegal.

cards.front: What equipment does a bicycle need at night?
cards.back: A bicycle ridden at night needs a white headlamp that can be seen from five hundred feet and a rear reflector.

cards.front: What can make a bicyclist easier for drivers to see?
cards.back: A flashing red light on the back of a bicycle can make the rider easier for drivers to see.

cards.front: What do the three feet and five hundred feet figures for bicycles measure?
cards.back: The three feet figure is the minimum gap when passing a bicyclist, while the five hundred feet figure is how far away a bicycle's white night headlamp must be visible.

cards.front: How does the two abreast limit differ from the passenger limit?
cards.back: The limit on riding two abreast is about how many bicycles ride side by side, while the passenger limit is about how many people one bicycle may carry.

cards.front: Which bicycle night lights are required, and which is optional?
cards.back: A white headlamp and a rear reflector are required on a bicycle at night, while a flashing red rear light is an optional way to be seen better.

decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: In a crash, who is more likely to be injured, a motorcyclist or a car driver?
cards.back: In a crash, a motorcyclist is more likely to be injured than the driver of a car.

cards.front: How do most crashes between cars and motorcycles happen?
cards.back: Most crashes between cars and motorcycles happen when a car turns in front of a motorcycle, usually because the driver did not see it or misjudged its distance and speed.

cards.front: How can a motorcycle's small size fool a driver?
cards.back: A motorcycle's small size can make it hard to spot and can make it look farther away and slower than it really is.

cards.front: Why is a motorcycle's distance harder to judge by its lights?
cards.back: A motorcycle's single headlight or taillight gives you fewer clues for judging its distance.

cards.front: In what weather are motorcyclists less stable?
cards.back: Motorcyclists are less stable in rain and wind.

cards.front: What is lane filtering?
cards.back: Lane filtering is when a motorcyclist safely passes a vehicle that is stopped in the same lane and direction.

cards.front: How many lanes must a street have for lane filtering?
cards.back: Lane filtering is allowed only on a street with at least two adjacent lanes going the same direction.

cards.front: What posted speed limit allows lane filtering?
cards.back: Lane filtering is allowed only where the posted speed limit is no higher than forty-five miles per hour.

cards.front: How fast may a motorcycle go while lane filtering?
cards.back: While lane filtering, the motorcycle may not go faster than fifteen miles per hour.

cards.front: For lane filtering, what are the posted speed limit and the motorcycle's top speed?
cards.back: For lane filtering, the posted limit may be no higher than forty-five miles per hour, while the motorcycle itself may go no faster than fifteen miles per hour.

cards.front: What two conditions describe lane filtering?
cards.back: Lane filtering means passing a vehicle stopped in the same lane, and it also needs at least two adjacent lanes going the same direction.

cards.front: How does misjudging a motorcycle lead to crashes?
cards.back: A motorcycle tends to look farther away and slower than it really is, which is why drivers turning in front of motorcycles cause most car and motorcycle crashes.

decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: Where is the risk of car and motorcycle collisions high?
cards.back: Intersections carry a high risk of car and motorcycle collisions, usually because a driver turns into the motorcycle's path.

cards.front: When a rider moves to one side, should you assume a turn?
cards.back: Do not assume what a rider intends, since a rider may move to one side to avoid a hazard or to be seen, not only to get ready to turn.

cards.front: Why might a motorcycle come into your lane unexpectedly?
cards.back: Motorcyclists may shift within their lane to avoid oil, potholes or debris, so a motorcycle may come into your lane unexpectedly.

cards.front: Why must you be certain of a rider's plan before pulling into a motorcycle's path?
cards.back: Motorcycle turn signals do not cancel themselves, so be certain of the rider's plan before you pull into the motorcycle's path.

cards.front: How much of a lane is a motorcycle entitled to?
cards.back: A motorcycle is entitled to the full width of a lane, so never squeeze into the same lane as a motorcycle.

cards.front: What can happen if you cut back too early after passing a motorcycle?
cards.back: After passing a motorcycle, cutting back into your lane too early can push the rider to swerve into other traffic or off the road.

cards.front: Why might a rider move to one side or show a blinking signal without turning?
cards.back: A rider moving to one side may be avoiding a hazard rather than turning, and a blinking motorcycle signal may simply have been left on after a turn.

decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: Why do large trucks matter to the Arizona economy?
cards.back: Large trucks matter to the Arizona economy because they carry products people depend on.

cards.front: Why should you never cut in front of a truck?
cards.back: Never cut in front of a truck, because a truck needs twice as long to stop.

cards.front: What happens if you cut in front of a truck and then brake hard?
cards.back: If you cut in front of a truck and then brake hard, you cut the truck's available stopping distance in half.

cards.front: What is the No-Zone, and what should you avoid there?
cards.back: Large trucks and buses have big blind spots, called the No-Zone, at the front and along the back sides, so do not linger there.

cards.front: Why should you follow a truck at a safe distance?
cards.back: Follow a truck at a safe distance, since a truck is almost as wide as some lanes and following too closely leaves you no time to react.

cards.front: Why should you never pass a truck on the right if it might turn right?
cards.back: Trucks make wide right turns and may leave an open space on their right just before turning, so never pass a truck on the right if it might turn right.

cards.front: If you break down, where should you pull your car?
cards.back: If you break down, pull as far off the highway as you can, because a parked car hit on the shoulder suffers more severe damage.

cards.front: How much can a truck weigh, measured in cars?
cards.back: A truck can weigh as much as twenty-five cars, so a truck striking a car parked on the shoulder could be tragic.

cards.front: How do twice as long and half the distance apply to trucks?
cards.back: A truck needs twice as long to stop, and cutting in front of it then braking leaves it only half its stopping distance.
cards.memory_hook: twice to stop, half cut off

decks.domain: Sharing the road with bicyclists, motorcycles, trucks and slow-moving vehicles, plus the last light rail cautions for children

cards.front: How should you follow farm machinery and other slow-moving vehicles?
cards.back: Behind farm machinery and other slow-moving vehicles, keep a safe following distance that gives you a good field of vision.

cards.front: How fast does farm machinery normally move?
cards.back: Farm machinery normally moves at twenty-five miles per hour or slower, can occupy more than one lane and may lack signals.

cards.front: How may a farm machinery operator make a wide right turn?
cards.back: To make a wide turn, a farm machinery operator may pull to the left first and then turn to the right.

cards.front: What is the top speed of a vehicle showing the slow-moving vehicle symbol, and what should you do?
cards.back: A vehicle showing the slow-moving vehicle symbol on its back cannot go faster than twenty-five miles per hour, so the symbol is your signal to slow down.

cards.front: Does a slow-moving vehicle have a right to be on the road?
cards.back: A slow-moving vehicle has a legal right to be on the road, so do not grow impatient when you are behind one.

cards.front: How does a truck's wide right turn differ from a farm machine's wide turn?
cards.back: A truck's wide right turn may leave open space on its right that you must not pass into, while a farm machine may pull left before turning right.

cards.front: How do farm machinery's usual speed and the slow-moving vehicle limit compare?
cards.back: Farm machinery usually travels at twenty-five miles per hour or less, while a vehicle with the slow-moving vehicle symbol can never exceed twenty-five miles per hour

recap_hooks.text: Bicyclists follow the same laws, so pass with at least three feet, never honk, dim your lights and expect legal moves left.
Bicyclists ride with traffic near the right, at most two abreast, and need a white headlamp and rear reflector at night.
Motorcycles look farther and slower than they are; lane filtering needs two adjacent lanes, a posted limit of forty-five or lower, and fifteen at most.
Do not assume a rider's plan, give the motorcycle the full lane, and do not cut back in too early after passing.
Trucks need twice as long to stop, have a No-Zone, make wide right turns and can weigh as much as twenty-five cars.
Farm machinery usually goes twenty-five or slower, may pull left before turning right, and has a right to the road.
